title: Min Max Riddle
directAnswer: For each window size w from 1..n, output the maximum over all length-w windows of that window's minimum. Don't enumerate windows. Instead, for each element find the largest window in which it is the minimum (its span between the previous-smaller and next-smaller elements) using a monotonic stack; that element is a candidate answer for that span length. Take the max per length, then sweep from large lengths down to small so every size inherits the best of any larger feasible span. O(n).

remember.pattern: Monotonic stack → span where each element is the minimum
rules: Each element `arr[i]` is the minimum of every window contained in its span `(prevSmaller, nextSmaller)`; the largest such window has length `nextSmaller − prevSmaller − 1`.
An element that is the answer for window length L is also a valid candidate for every length **smaller** than L — hence the final descending sweep.
Compute previous-smaller and next-smaller indices with a **monotonic increasing stack**, popping while the stacked value is `≥` the current value.
Use a boundary of `-1` on the left and `n` on the right for elements with no smaller neighbour.
Answer array is 1-indexed by window size; `ans[w]` is the result for windows of size `w`.
whenToUse: 'For every window size, the max/min of window mins/maxes' style aggregate queries
You need the span in which each element dominates as the min (or max)
Histogram / largest-rectangle relatives where each bar's reach matters
Any time brute force is O(n²) over windows and you want O(n) via spans
antiSignals: A single fixed window size → sliding-window deque (Sliding Window Maximum), not per-size spans
You need the actual windows, not just the aggregate → spans don't reconstruct them directly
Values can repeat heavily and you need exact counts → be careful with ≥ vs > to avoid double-count
remember.takeaway: Replace 'iterate every window' with 'for each element, what is the largest window where it's the minimum?'. A monotonic stack gives every element's span in O(n); a descending max-sweep then fills all smaller sizes. This span-of-dominance idea powers Largest Rectangle and Sum of Subarray Minimums too.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can flip an O(n²)-over-windows problem into an O(n) per-element span computation with a monotonic stack, and reason about the 'a length-L answer also serves all smaller lengths' sweep.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Brute-forcing all windows (TLE for n up to 10⁵), getting the span boundaries wrong, or forgetting the descending sweep so smaller window sizes are left too small.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Name the previous-smaller / next-smaller monotonic-stack technique, explain why the largest span an element wins as min answers that length, and justify the descending max-propagation in one sentence.

problemStatement:
You are given an array `arr` of `n` integers. For a window (contiguous subarray) you take its minimum. For every window **size** from 1 to n, consider all windows of that size and take the **maximum** of their minimums.

Return an array of `n` values where the value at index `w − 1` is the maximum-of-minimums over all windows of size `w`.
constraints: Output has exactly n values (one per window size 1..n)
An O(n²) solution times out — O(n) or O(n log n) is required
understanding: For each window length we want the best (largest) achievable minimum. A large element can only be a window's minimum inside the stretch where no smaller element intrudes — that stretch is its 'span'. The longest window in which arr[i] is the minimum has length equal to the distance between the nearest strictly-smaller elements on each side. That length is the largest window size for which arr[i] is a candidate answer; it also qualifies for all shorter sizes.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Output one value per window size, 1 through n?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — n values total. Index 0 is window size 1 (the global max element), index n−1 is window size n (the global min).

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can values repeat?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. Handle ties consistently in the stack (pop on ≥) so a run of equal values isn't double-counted in spans.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the largest window size's answer just the global minimum?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. The only window of size n is the whole array, whose minimum is the array's minimum.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Why does a length-L answer also count for smaller lengths?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: If arr[i] is the minimum of some length-L window, it's also the minimum of sub-windows of that window of every smaller size, so it remains a candidate for those sizes.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Every Window of Every Size
approaches.whenToMention: State it to anchor the problem, then immediately note it's O(n²) (or O(n³) naively) and will TLE for n = 10⁵.
hints: Directly translate the definition: for each window size w, slide a window across and track its minimum.
Maintaining the running minimum as the window slides keeps each size at O(n), giving O(n²) overall.
n up to 10⁵ means n² ≈ 10¹⁰ operations — far too slow. This frames why we need the stack approach.
approaches.complexityReasoning: n window sizes × O(n) work to scan windows of that size = O(n²). With a naive inner min recomputation it degrades to O(n³).
approaches.explanation:
The literal reading: for each window size `w` from 1 to n, examine every length-`w` window, compute its minimum, and keep the maximum of those minimums.

**Why it's the natural first attempt.** It mirrors the problem statement one-to-one — two nested loops over (size, start position) plus a min. There's no insight required, just enumeration.

**Making the inner min cheap.** For a fixed size, sliding the window one step changes only the entering and leaving elements. A monotonic deque tracks the window minimum in amortised O(1), so each size is O(n) and the whole thing is O(n²). Without that, recomputing the min from scratch makes it O(n³).

**Why we don't ship it.** At n = 10⁵, O(n²) is ~10¹⁰ operations — a guaranteed timeout. It's useful only as a correctness oracle to test the optimal solution against on small inputs.
approaches.insight: Brute force re-derives each window's minimum independently and so repeats enormous work. The optimal flips the question: rather than 'what is each window's min?', ask 'for each element, which windows is it the min of?' — answered once per element with a stack.

approaches.name: Monotonic Stack — Span of Dominance (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The intended solution. Explain previous-smaller / next-smaller spans and the descending max-sweep.
hints: Instead of asking each window for its minimum, ask each element: what is the longest window in which I am the minimum?
An element stays the minimum until a strictly smaller element appears on its left or right. Find the nearest smaller element on each side with a monotonic stack.

If arr[i]'s span (between nearest smaller neighbours) has length L, then arr[i] is a candidate answer for window size L — and for every size below L. Take per-size maxima, then propagate from large sizes down to small.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each element is pushed and popped from the stack at most once across both passes → O(n). The final descending sweep is O(n). Arrays of size n → O(n) space.
approaches.explanation:
Turn the problem inside out. Rather than computing each window's minimum, determine for each element the *largest window in which it is the minimum*.

**The span of an element.** `arr[i]` is the minimum of a window exactly while no smaller value is inside that window. So extend left until you hit the nearest element strictly smaller than `arr[i]` (call its index `prevSmaller[i]`), and right until the nearest strictly smaller element (`nextSmaller[i]`). The widest window where `arr[i]` reigns as minimum has length `len = nextSmaller[i] − prevSmaller[i] − 1`.

**Computing prev/next smaller in O(n).** A monotonic increasing stack does both. Scanning left to right, before pushing `i` we pop every index whose value is `≥ arr[i]`; whatever remains on top is the previous strictly-smaller element (or `−1` if the stack empties). A symmetric right-to-left scan gives `nextSmaller` (boundary `n`). Each index is pushed and popped once, so it's linear.

**Mapping spans to answers.** For each `i`, `arr[i]` is a valid candidate for window size `len`. Record `ans[len] = max(ans[len], arr[i])`. Multiple elements can share a length; we keep the largest.

**The descending sweep — the subtle finish.** An element that is the minimum of a length-`L` window is also the minimum of sub-windows of every smaller size within it, so it is a candidate for all sizes `≤ L`. After filling `ans[len]` directly, sweep from `w = n−1` down to `1` doing `ans[w] = max(ans[w], ans[w+1])`. This lets a strong answer found at a large length flow down to fill any smaller size that didn't get a bigger candidate of its own.

**Handling ties.** Popping on `≥` (not `>`) in both passes assigns each window of equal-valued runs to a single representative, preventing a value from being counted as the minimum of an overlapping span twice. The per-size max is unaffected because the true best still wins, but it keeps spans clean.
approaches.insight: The pivot from 'minimum of each window' to 'span where each element is the minimum' is the entire trick — and it's the same monotonic-stack span idea behind Largest Rectangle in Histogram and Sum of Subarray Minimums. Once you see 'nearest smaller on both sides', a whole family of O(n²)-looking problems collapse to O(n).

pitfalls: Mixing up the span formula — it's nextSmaller − prevSmaller − 1, not nextSmaller − prevSmaller.
Skipping the descending sweep — smaller window sizes are left at 0 or too small.
Using > instead of ≥ inconsistently across the two passes, double-counting equal runs.
Sweeping in ascending order — answers must flow from large sizes DOWN to small ones.
Using int sums for values up to 10⁹ where products overflow (here we only compare, so long is safe; still prefer long).

edgeCases.behavior: With ≥-pops, spans give ans[1]=4 and the whole-array min sweep yields [4, 4].
Increasing: element 5 has span 1, element 1 span 5 → [5, 4, 3, 2, 1].

commonMistakes: Enumerating all windows (O(n²)/O(n³)) and timing out for large n.
Getting the span length formula wrong (off-by-one on the boundaries).
Forgetting the descending max-sweep that fills smaller window sizes.
Inconsistent tie handling (≥ vs >) across the previous-smaller and next-smaller passes.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Skipping the descending sweep
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Directly assigning ans[span] only fills the exact largest length each element wins. Smaller sizes that lack their own large candidate stay zero. A length-L answer is valid for all sizes ≤ L, so you must propagate downward.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
for i in range(n):
    length = next_smaller[i] - prev_smaller[i] - 1
    ans[length] = max(ans[length], arr[i])
return ans[1:n + 1]   # smaller sizes may still be 0

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Wrong span boundary formula
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The span counts elements strictly between the two smaller neighbours. Using nextSmaller − prevSmaller overcounts by one and misassigns elements to a window size one too large.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
int len = nextSmaller[i] - prevSmaller[i];      // off by one
ans[len] = Math.max(ans[len], arr[i]);
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
int len = nextSmaller[i] - prevSmaller[i] - 1;
ans[len] = Math.max(ans[len], arr[i]);

patternNote: Monotonic-stack span-of-dominance: for each element find the nearest strictly-smaller neighbours, derive the largest window it's the min of, then propagate answers from large window sizes down to small. Same machinery as Largest Rectangle and Sum of Subarray Minimums.
